catalog_quote: Like in Standard Chinese, the lexical stress in Nanchang is realized on disyllabic words where the first syllable is a full syllable and the second syllable is a light syllable known as ‘qing sheng’ (Chao 1968). Perceptually, native speakers can tell that the first syllable is more prominent than the second syllable. ... In disyllabic words, only the second syllable can be lexically stressless. The presence or absence of lexical stress on the second syllable sometimes may distinguish the meanings of two words: (1a) toŋ42 ɕi42 ‘east west’ (1b) toŋ42 ɕi ‘thing’. In (1a), the syllables are “full-full” and it is not easy for native speakers to tell which has more stress. In (1b), the syllables are “full-light” and the first syllable is judged to be more stressed than the second syllable by native speakers. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Nanchang Gan is a tone language (five citation tones). Word-level prominence is a full-syllable vs. light-syllable (qingsheng, toneless/reduced) contrast: a light syllable can only be the non-initial (second) syllable of a disyllable, giving strong-weak words, and which words have a light second syllable is lexically listed, not rule-governed; in full-full words speakers perceive no clear stress difference. Above the word, 'grammatical stress' follows Duanmu's Nonhead Stress: N1 is stressed in [N1 N2] compounds (initial), N in [V N] phrases (final), supported by speaker judgments, blocking of 213-tone sandhi on stressed N1, and longer rhyme durations (p. 8: 'in Nanchang, a [V N] phrase has grammatical stress on N and a [N1 N2] compound has grammatical stress on N1').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; the thesis distinguishes three prominence grades instrumentally (grammatically stressed > lexically stressed but grammatically stressless > lexically stressless/light), with rhyme duration as correlate and tonal inventory reduced from 5 to 2 on light syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Full-light membership is lexically idiosyncratic and differs from the Standard Chinese neutral-tone lexicon; checked (CVO) syllables are short regardless of stress; Sagart 1999 adds that lexicalized T0 items are typically grammatical morphemes and that restressing a T0 syllable yields tone 7; Sagart 1989 (Shanggao Gan) states an atonic syllable is never the first syllable of a polysyllabic morpheme.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level = disyllabic words (full vs light second syllable); compound/phrase level = Nonhead Stress ([N N] initial, [V N] final). Data are elicited disyllables in a carrier context plus native-speaker prominence judgments; variety is urban Nanchang.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Nanchang city Gan (南昌话, the prestige/reference variety of Gan, Chang-Du subgroup); Glottolog treats Gan (ganc1239) at language level with Nanchang as its usual reference point. Supporting first-hand notes: Sagart 1999 (also Nanchang) and Sagart 1989 (Shanggao, Yi-Liu subgroup). Li Xuping 2018 (not opened) describes Yichun Gan (Yi-Liu subgroup). Zhang Shengkai's TUFS work is on Pingjiang (Hunan), a peripheral Gan variety.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1.1-1.1.2 (pp.2-8): Nanchang is a tone language (5 tones); 'lexical stress' = full vs light (qingsheng) syllables; in disyllables only the 2nd syllable can be lexically stressless, first syllable judged more prominent; full-full words: speakers cannot tell which is more stressed; full-light pattern not predictable, lexically specified; 'grammatical stress' by Duanmu's Nonhead Stress: N stressed in [V N] phrases, N1 in [N1 N2] compounds (supported by speaker judgments, tone-sandhi blocking and rhyme-duration measurements); tonal inventory reduced to 2 in stressless syllables.

sources.citation: Sagart, Laurent. 1999. Notes on Nanchang dialect (draft). Ms., Melbourne; HAL hal-00410000 (deposited 2009), 112 pp.
sources.note: p.3 (1.1.1 Tones): 7 tones plus 'a qingsheng (T0)... for de- or unstressed syllables, which are also typically reduced for their rhyme'; T0 contour depends on preceding tone (after Wei & Chen 1998); 'Destressing can be due to speech environment but some morphemes (typically grammatical morphemes...) have lexicalized T0'; restressing of T0 yields T7. No positional word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Sagart, Laurent. 1989. Phonologie et lexique d'un dialecte Gan: Shanggao. Cahiers de linguistique - Asie orientale 18(2): 183-227.
sources.note: p.187 (3.3.1): 'Toutes les syllabes portent un ton, à l'exception de quelques syllabes atones' (high level [44]/[55]); atonic syllables may be suffixes or reduplicants; 'Une syllabe atone n'est jamais la première d'un morphème polysyllabique'; several atonics can follow each other. Also a floating high 'H' tone affix on last syllable of nouns (pp.188-189). No statement on stress/accent as such.
